subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalaamu alaykum, and welcome to your very first science unit of Year 3! In this unit you are going to become a real scientist. A scientist is simply a person who looks carefully at the world, asks good questions, and tries to find true answers. You already do this every day without even knowing it. When you wonder why the camel by your house chews all day, or why the acacia tree grows new green leaves after the rains come, you are thinking like a scientist.

objectives.text: Know life processes common to humans and animals include nutrition (water and food), movement, growth and reproduction
Describe differences between living and non-living things using knowledge of life processes
Explain observations that plants need water and light to grow

outcomes: Sort things into three groups: living, dead, and never-alive — and explain why.
Name and describe the seven life processes that every living thing does (we call them MRS GREN).
Explain how a plant makes its own food and gives off the oxygen that you and every animal breathe.
Describe how a seed wakes up and grows into a new plant — a process called germination.
Give reasons using science words, not just guesses, for every answer you make.
Plan and do a safe, careful investigation at home using things from your own kitchen.
Connect what plants and animals need to what you and your own family need every day.

concepts.title: The Three Groups: Living, Dead, and Never-Alive
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin our science adventure with a walk. Imagine you step outside your home in the early morning, when the air is cool and the sky is turning gold. What do you see? Maybe a goat chewing quietly. Maybe an acacia tree with long thorns. Maybe a stone by the path, a metal gate, a puddle of water, and a dried brown leaf that fell in the night. All of these things are around you — but they are not the same kind of thing. Some are alive, some used to be alive, and some were never alive at all.

A living thing is alive right now. The goat breathes, moves, eats grass, and can have baby goats. The acacia tree is also living — it drinks water through its roots, grows taller each season, and makes seeds. Even though the tree cannot walk away like the goat, it is just as alive. This is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit: plants are living things, just like animals. Many people forget this, because plants are quiet and still. But quiet does not mean lifeless.

A dead thing was alive before, but it has stopped. That dried brown leaf on the path was once a green living leaf, joined to a tree, drinking water and catching sunlight. Now it has fallen, dried up, and stopped doing the jobs of life. It is dead. A wooden stool is also dead — it is made from a tree that was cut down. Goat meat, a leather sandal, and a cotton dress are all dead too, because they all came from things that were once living. This can be surprising! Your clothes were once alive as a cotton plant in a field.

A never-alive thing has never been alive, not even once. A rock has always been a rock. A metal spoon was dug from the ground as ore and shaped by people. Water in a well is never-alive. A plastic bucket, a glass window, a clay pot — none of these has ever eaten, grown, breathed, or had babies. They cannot die, because they were never alive to begin with. This is the difference many children find trickiest: dead is not the same as never-alive. Dead things had a life once; never-alive things never did.

Did You Know? The cotton in a shirt, the wood in a door, the leather in a sandal, and the paper in a book were all once alive! Cotton was a plant, wood was a tree, leather came from an animal, and paper is made from trees. So many things in your home began their story as living things.
concepts.example: Here is a gentle way to remember the difference. Ask yourself two small questions about the thing in front of you. First: Is it doing the jobs of life right now — breathing, feeding, growing? If yes, it is living. If no, ask the second question: Did it ever do the jobs of life, or did it come from something that did? If yes, it is dead. If it never did and never came from anything alive, it is never-alive. These two questions will guide you through almost every puzzle in this unit.

concepts.title: The Seven Life Processes (MRS GREN)
concepts.explanation:
How do scientists know for sure whether something is alive? They do not just guess. They check a special list of seven jobs that every single living thing must do. Every plant, every animal, every person, and even the tiniest creature too small to see does all seven of these jobs. If something does all seven, it is alive. Scientists call these the seven life processes.

Seven things are a lot to remember, so scientists made a clever nickname to help. Take the first letter of each process and you can spell out the name of a made-up person: MRS GREN. She is not a real lady, but she is a wonderful memory helper. Say her name a few times and you will never forget the seven life processes. Let us meet each letter.

All living things move in some way. This is easy to see with animals. A cheetah runs across the savanna, a flamingo wades in the water, a fish flicks its tail, and a camel plods along the dusty road. But what about plants? Plants cannot walk, yet they truly do move. A sunflower slowly turns its face to follow the sun across the sky. A bean shoot bends toward a window. A flower opens its petals in the morning and closes them at night. The movement is slow and gentle, so slow that you cannot see it happen while you watch — but if you check the plant morning and evening, you will see that it has moved. Movement in plants is usually growing movement, and it is real movement all the same.

Respiration is a big word for a hidden job that happens inside every living thing, all day and all night. Respiration means releasing energy from food. Your body takes the food you eat, like bariis and goat meat, and uses oxygen to unlock the energy trapped inside it. That energy lets you run, think, and grow. Be careful here: respiration is not the same as breathing! Breathing is moving air in and out. Respiration is the quiet work happening deep inside your cells. Even plants respire — day and night they release energy from their own food to stay alive. Respiration is happening inside you at this very moment.

Sensitivity means noticing changes around you and responding to them. When bright sunlight hits your face, your eyes squint — that is sensitivity. When you touch a hot pot, you pull your hand away quickly — that is sensitivity too. Animals have amazing senses: a goat hears a lion and runs, a camel smells water far away in the desert. Plants are sensitive as well. Roots sense which way is down and grow downward. Leaves sense the sun and turn toward it. The touch-me-not plant folds its leaves the moment you touch them. Every living thing keeps sensing its world and answering it.

Every living thing grows. You were once a tiny baby, and now you are much bigger and can do so much more. A newborn goat kid is small and wobbly, but it grows into a strong adult goat. A tiny seed grows into a towering mango tree that can feed a whole family for years. Growth means getting bigger and also developing new parts — a plant grows new leaves and flowers, and you grow new teeth. Never-alive things do not grow like this. A rock does not get bigger by eating and using food; it only breaks into smaller pieces. True growth comes from the living thing building itself using food.

Reproduction means making new living things of the same kind. Goats have baby goats, camels have baby camels, and people have babies. This is how each kind of living thing continues and does not disappear from the world. Plants reproduce too, but in their own way. A mango tree makes flowers, and the flowers make seeds inside the fruit. When a seed lands in good soil, it can grow into a brand new mango tree. Without reproduction, there would be no new goats, no new trees, and no new people. It is one of the most important signs of life.

As living things use food and energy, they make waste — leftover things the body does not need and must remove. Getting rid of this waste is called excretion. When you sweat on a hot day in Mogadishu, you are excreting. Animals excrete waste too. Plants also make waste and get rid of it. Interestingly, when a plant makes its food, it gives off a gas as waste — and that gas is oxygen, the very gas that keeps you alive! So one living thing's waste can be another living thing's treasure. Excretion keeps the inside of a living body clean and healthy.

Nutrition means getting food. Every living thing needs food for energy and for growing. But there are two different ways to get food. Animals, including you, must eat other things — a lion eats meat, a goat eats grass, and you eat rice, milk, and dates. Plants are special: they do not eat at all. Instead, they make their own food from sunlight, water, and air. This amazing plant power is called photosynthesis, and we will explore it closely in the next part. So both plants and animals have nutrition, but plants are the clever cooks who make their own meals.

Did You Know? The tiny creatures that make yoghurt and that live in a drop of pond water are alive too! They are far too small to see with just your eyes, yet they still do all seven life processes — they move, feed, grow, and even reproduce. Life is happening everywhere, even in places we cannot see.

Now here is a clever thinking tip. To decide if something is alive, you do not always have to see all seven processes with your own eyes at the same time. Some, like respiration, are hidden inside. Instead, scientists ask: could this thing do all seven if we watched it long enough and looked closely enough? A sleeping goat is not moving much and is not eating right now, but it can do all seven, so it is alive. This careful thinking is what makes you a true young scientist.
concepts.example: Let us also think about why MRS GREN works for such different living things. A tiny ant, a tall giraffe, a green acacia tree, and you yourself all look completely different. Yet every single one does the same seven jobs. This is one of the amazing patterns in Allah's creation: no matter how big or small, no matter whether it swims, walks, or stands rooted in the soil, a living thing always shows these same seven signs of life. When you notice the same pattern appearing again and again in nature, you are thinking exactly like a real scientist. Patterns help us understand and remember the world.

concepts.title: How Plants Make Food and Give Us Air to Breathe
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to one of the most wonderful secrets in all of science. You need food to live, and you get it by eating. But a plant never eats a single meal — and yet it grows from a tiny seed into a giant baobab tree. How can this be? The answer is that a plant is a food factory. It makes its own food from things it gathers around itself. This process is called photosynthesis, which is a long word that simply means "making things with light."

To make its food, a green plant needs three ingredients, like a cook needs ingredients for canjeero. First, it needs water, which it drinks up through its roots from the soil. Second, it needs a gas from the air called carbon dioxide, which it takes in through tiny holes in its leaves. Third, and most important, it needs sunlight, which it catches with its green leaves. The green colour of leaves is special — it is what lets the plant trap the sun's energy.

Inside the leaf, something amazing happens. The plant uses the energy from sunlight to mix the water and carbon dioxide together and turn them into sugar, which is the plant's food. This sugar gives the plant energy to grow tall, make flowers, and produce seeds and fruit. When you eat a sweet mango or a date, you are tasting the sugar that a plant made using sunlight! That sweetness is captured sunshine.

But photosynthesis has a second gift, and it is a gift for you. When the plant finishes making its food, it has some leftover gas it does not need. That leftover gas is oxygen — and the plant lets it go out into the air. Oxygen is the exact gas that you, and goats, and camels, and fish, and every animal must breathe to stay alive. So every green leaf on every mango tree, every blade of grass, and every water plant in the Jubba River is quietly making the air that keeps you breathing. Isn't that a beautiful design in Allah's creation?

The Simple Recipe for Photosynthesis Water (from the soil) + Carbon dioxide (from the air) + Sunlight (caught by green leaves) gives us: Sugar (the plant's food) + Oxygen (the gas we breathe out into the air). Plants take a gas we do not want and give back the gas we need. What a gift!
concepts.example: Now think about this. You breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. A plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen. Do you see how you and plants are perfect partners? You give plants the gas they need, and plants give you the gas you need. This is why planting trees and caring for green things is so important. When people cut down too many trees, there are fewer leaves to make oxygen and clean the air. Caring for plants is caring for the breath of every living thing.

concepts.title: Seeds and Germination: New Life Begins
concepts.explanation:
Have you ever soaked beans overnight to cook them, and noticed that after a day or two they start to sprout a tiny white tail? That tiny tail is the beginning of a brand new plant! The waking up of a seed and the start of its growth is called germination. It is one of the clearest ways to see the life process of reproduction and growth happening right in front of your eyes.

A seed may look small, hard, and lifeless, like a little stone. But do not be fooled — inside every seed is a tiny sleeping baby plant, packed together with a small store of food to help it start growing. The seed waits patiently, sometimes for a long time, until the conditions are just right. In the dry season, seeds in the soil rest and wait. Then, when the rains finally come, the whole land turns green because thousands of resting seeds wake up together and germinate.

What does a seed need to wake up and germinate? It needs water to soften its hard coat and wake the baby plant inside. It needs warmth, which is why seeds sprout well in the warm East African soil. And it needs air, because even a sprouting seed must respire. Notice one surprising thing: a seed does not need light to begin germinating. That first little root pushes down into the dark soil before the plant ever sees the sun. Light becomes important a little later, once the green shoot reaches up into the air.

When a seed germinates, the first part to appear is usually the root, which grows downward to find water and to hold the plant firmly in the ground. The root grows down because it can sense the pull of gravity — remember sensitivity from MRS GREN! After the root, a shoot pushes upward toward the light, and it opens the plant's first tiny leaves. Once those green leaves reach the sunlight, the young plant can begin photosynthesis and make its own food. From then on it can grow strong all by itself.

Did You Know? Some seeds can rest in dry soil for many years and still be alive inside, just waiting. The moment enough rain falls, they wake up and germinate. This is how the dry savanna bursts into green so quickly after the first big rains of the season.
concepts.example: Germination is a beautiful example of the whole story of this unit joining together. A seed is made through reproduction. It germinates and shows growth. Its root shows sensitivity by sensing gravity. It respires to release energy. Once it opens its leaves, it begins nutrition through photosynthesis and gives off oxygen through excretion. In one small sprouting bean, you can watch nearly all seven life processes begin. This is why scientists love watching seeds grow — it is life itself, starting fresh.

concepts.title: Guided Exploration — Think It Through
concepts.explanation:
Let us slow down and think together like scientists. Read each question, pause, and try to answer it in your own words before you read on. There is no rush. Thinking carefully is more important than answering fast.

Your friend Yusuf says, "A car must be alive because it moves and it drinks fuel like an animal drinks water." Using MRS GREN, how would you gently explain to Yusuf why a car is not alive? (Hint: can a car grow, reproduce, or have baby cars?)

Halima found a beautiful white seashell on the beach at Berbera. Is the shell living, dead, or never-alive? Think carefully — a shell was made by a living sea creature. What do you decide?

Why can a mango tree be alive even though it never moves from its spot and never eats a meal? Which of its life processes can you still find?

If all the green plants on Earth disappeared, what would happen to the air that animals and people breathe? Explain using what you learned about photosynthesis.
concepts.example: A bean seed and a small stone look almost the same size. You put both in warm, wet soil. After a week, one has changed completely and one looks the same. What happened, and what does this tell you about which one is alive?

concepts.title: Worked Example — Being a Classification Detective
concepts.explanation:
When scientists sort things, they follow careful steps instead of guessing. Let us solve one puzzle together, step by step, so you can see how a real scientist thinks. Our mystery object is a wooden stool in the corner of the room.

Step 1 — Look closely. The stool is made of hard, brown wood. It has grain lines running through it. It does not move on its own and feels dry.

Step 2 — Ask: is it doing the life processes now? Is the stool growing? No. Is it eating, breathing, or making baby stools? No. So it is not living right now.

Step 3 — Ask: was it ever alive, or did it come from something alive? Yes! Wood comes from a tree, and a tree is a living thing. The tree was cut down and shaped into a stool.

Step 4 — Decide. Because the stool came from a once-living tree but is not alive now, the stool is dead, not never-alive.

Step 5 — Explain your reasoning. "The stool is dead because it is made of wood, and wood comes from a tree that was once a living thing. It is not never-alive, because never-alive things like rocks and metal never came from anything living."

Do you see how the answer becomes clear when you follow the steps? Now try the very same five steps on a metal spoon, a growing onion, and a dried fish. Say each step out loud. This is exactly how you will earn top marks in the Practice book — not by guessing, but by explaining your reasoning like a real scientist.

methods.title: Wake Up a Seed (Germination)
methods.example: To watch a seed germinate and discover what a seed needs to wake up and start growing.
steps: Put a thick layer of damp cotton wool or paper towel inside each jar.
Place 4 or 5 beans between the cotton and the glass, where you can see them clearly.
Label the jars: Jar A gets water, Jar B stays dry.
For Jar A, keep the cotton damp each day (not flooded). Give Jar B no water at all.
Put both jars in a warm place with some light. Check them at the same time every day for one week.

methods.title: Does a Plant Follow the Light?
methods.example: To find out if a plant can move and respond to the direction of light (a life process called sensitivity).
steps: Place your potted plant on a windowsill where light comes from one side only.
Put a mark on the side of the pot facing the window so you remember its position.
Look at which way the leaves and stem are pointing and write it down.
Leave the plant for three days, keeping the soil lightly damp.
On day four, look again. Then turn the pot halfway around and watch over the next two days.

methods.title: The Classification Detective Hunt
methods.example: To practise sorting real objects into living, dead, and never-alive, and to explain your reasoning like a scientist.
steps: Collect your ten objects and place them all together in the middle of a table.
Pick up each object one at a time and look at it closely.
For each object, ask the two detective questions: Is it doing life processes now? Did it ever live or come from something living?
Place the object on the correct sheet: Living, Dead, or Never-alive.
In your notebook, write one sentence of reasoning for each object.

methods.title: Do Plants Breathe Out? (Bubbles of Life)
methods.example: To look for signs that a green water plant gives off a gas (oxygen) when it sits in the sunlight.
steps: Fill the clear bowl with room-temperature water.
Push the fresh green stems down so the leaves are fully underwater.
Place the bowl on a bright, sunny windowsill.
Watch closely for 20 to 30 minutes. Look for tiny bubbles forming on the leaves.
Then move the bowl to a dark corner or cover it with a box, and compare the number of bubbles.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a living thing? a) a rock b) a camel c) a metal spoon d) a plastic bucket
workedExamples.solution: b) a camel. A camel does all seven life processes, so it is living. The others never lived.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which word list names the seven life processes? a) big, small, hot, cold, wet, dry, hard b) movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition c) red, blue, green, tall, short, round, flat d) happy, sad, tired, hungry, cold, warm, sleepy
workedExamples.solution: b) movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition. These are the seven life processes, remembered as MRS GREN.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: A dried acacia leaf on the ground is best described as: a) living b) dead c) never-alive d) a gas
workedExamples.solution: b) dead. The leaf was once alive on a tree but has stopped doing life processes, so it is dead — not never-alive.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is never-alive? a) a goat b) a mango tree c) a river stone d) a bean seed
workedExamples.solution: c) a river stone. A stone has never been alive. A goat, a tree, and a seed are all living.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and: a) oxygen b) carbon dioxide c) soil only d) milk
workedExamples.solution: b) carbon dioxide. Plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide from the air to make food.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: What gas do plants give off that animals need to breathe? a) carbon dioxide b) smoke c) oxygen d) steam
workedExamples.solution: c) oxygen. Plants give off oxygen, the gas animals and people breathe in to live.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: What is it called when a seed wakes up and starts to grow? a) reproduction b) germination c) excretion d) respiration
workedExamples.solution: b) germination. Germination is when a resting seed wakes up and begins to grow.

activities.title: Wake Up a Seed (Germination)
activities.materials: A handful of dried beans, lentils, or mung beans from the kitchen.; Two clear glass jars or clean plastic cups.; Cotton wool, or a folded paper towel, or a clean cloth.; Water.
steps: Put a thick layer of damp cotton wool or paper towel inside each jar.
Place 4 or 5 beans between the cotton and the glass, where you can see them clearly.
Label the jars: Jar A gets water, Jar B stays dry.
For Jar A, keep the cotton damp each day (not flooded). Give Jar B no water at all.
Put both jars in a warm place with some light. Check them at the same time every day for one week.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Does a Plant Follow the Light?
activities.materials: A small potted plant, or a bean seedling you grew in Experiment 1 planted in a cup of soil.; A sunny window ledge.; A small sticker or piece of tape to mark the pot.
steps: Place your potted plant on a windowsill where light comes from one side only.
Put a mark on the side of the pot facing the window so you remember its position.
Look at which way the leaves and stem are pointing and write it down.
Leave the plant for three days, keeping the soil lightly damp.
On day four, look again. Then turn the pot halfway around and watch over the next two days.

activities.title: The Classification Detective Hunt
activities.materials: Ten safe objects from around your home (for example: a houseplant leaf, a dried leaf, a wooden spoon, a metal spoon, a stone, a plastic cup, a piece of cloth, a fresh onion, a glass jar, a date).; Three sheets of paper labelled Living, Dead, and Never-alive.; Your science notebook and a pencil.
steps: Collect your ten objects and place them all together in the middle of a table.
Pick up each object one at a time and look at it closely.
For each object, ask the two detective questions: Is it doing life processes now? Did it ever live or come from something living?
Place the object on the correct sheet: Living, Dead, or Never-alive.
In your notebook, write one sentence of reasoning for each object.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Do Plants Breathe Out? (Bubbles of Life)
activities.materials: A clear glass bowl or large jar.; A few fresh green leafy stems (pondweed if you have any, or fresh leafy herbs like mint).; Water at room temperature.; A sunny windowsill.
steps: Fill the clear bowl with room-temperature water.
Push the fresh green stems down so the leaves are fully underwater.
Place the bowl on a bright, sunny windowsill.
Watch closely for 20 to 30 minutes. Look for tiny bubbles forming on the leaves.
Then move the bowl to a dark corner or cover it with a box, and compare the number of bubbles.

rules.title: The Seven Life Processes
rules.text: Remember! Every living thing does all SEVEN life processes: M — Movement R — Respiration S — Sensitivity G — Growth R — Reproduction E — Excretion N — Nutrition If something does all seven, it is ALIVE.

rules.title: Living, Dead or Never Alive
rules.text: Sorting Made Simple: LIVING: doing the life processes right now (a camel, a tree, you). DEAD: was once alive, or came from something alive, but has stopped (a dried leaf, wood, leather, meat). NEVER-ALIVE: never lived at all (rock, metal, plastic, glass, water). Key question: Did it ever live? If yes but not now, it is DEAD. If never, it is NEVER-ALIVE.

rules.title: The Photosynthesis Recipe
rules.text: The Recipe: Water + Carbon dioxide + Sunlight -> Sugar (plant food) + Oxygen (for us to breathe). Roots drink water. Leaves take in carbon dioxide and catch sunlight. The plant makes its own food and gives us the oxygen we breathe.

rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Germination is when a resting seed wakes up and begins to grow.

rounds.prompt: Which two words describe getting rid of waste, and making new living things?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: excretion and reproduction. Excretion is removing waste; reproduction is making new living things.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a living thing?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: a camel. A camel does all seven life processes, so it is living. The others never lived.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is never-alive?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: a river stone. A stone has never been alive. A goat, a tree, and a seed are all living.

games.description: Practise carbon dioxide through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: How does a plant show movement?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: it grows toward the light. Plants move slowly by growing, especially toward light.

rounds.prompt: MRS GREN is a way to remember:

rounds.prompt: Which word list names the seven life processes?
choices: big, small, hot, cold, wet, dry, hard
movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
red, blue, green, tall, short, round, flat
happy, sad, tired, hungry, cold, warm, sleepy
rounds.answer: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition. These are the seven life processes, remembered as MRS GREN.

rounds.prompt: Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: carbon dioxide. Plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide from the air to make food.

games.title: Real-Life Round: Germination
games.description: Practise germination through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which of these was once alive but is now dead?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: a wooden stool. Wood comes from a once-living tree, so the stool is dead. The others were never alive.

rounds.prompt: A goat eating grass is showing which life process?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: nutrition. Eating to get food and energy is the life process called nutrition.

rounds.prompt: A dried acacia leaf on the ground is best described as:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: dead. The leaf was once alive on a tree but has stopped doing life processes, so it is dead — not never-alive.

rounds.prompt: What gas do plants give off that animals need to breathe?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: oxygen. Plants give off oxygen, the gas animals and people breathe in to live.

selfAssessment: I can sort things into three groups: living, dead, and never-alive — and explain why.
I can name and describe the seven life processes that every living thing does (we call them MRS GREN).
I can explain how a plant makes its own food and gives off the oxygen that you and every animal breathe.
I can describe how a seed wakes up and grows into a new plant — a process called germination.
I can give reasons using science words, not just guesses, for every answer you make.
I can plan and do a safe, careful investigation at home using things from your own kitchen.
I can connect what plants and animals need to what you and your own family need every day.
